claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi corresponds approximately to Co20Cr20Fe20Ni20Ti20 in atomic percent.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can be retained as a single-phase solid solution with a uniform microstructure.
The relevant starting material has a low initial dislocation density.
Rapid quenching retains a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The low hardness and strength arise from a scarcity of obstacles to dislocation motion in the homogeneous single-phase state.
The homogeneous solid-solution environment reduces solute-dislocation interactions.
The absence of secondary-phase obstacles permits facile dislocation glide.
Deformation produces easy planar slip in the single-phase alloy.
Rapid dynamic recovery annihilates or rearranges dislocations during deformation.
Dynamic recovery prevents substantial dislocation accumulation.
Limited dislocation accumulation suppresses work hardening and yields low strength and hardness despite favorable plasticity.
At room temperature and moderate strain rates, the starting alloy will show early plastic yielding, low yield strength, and a low work-hardening rate.
TEM after deformation will show only a modest increase in dislocation density because recovery is effective.
Thermal aging can induce nanoscale precipitates in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates will hinder recovery and increase yield strength and hardness relative to the single-phase starting state.
Testing at lower temperatures will hinder recovery and increase yield strength and hardness.
The mechanism applies at ambient temperature and moderate strain rates while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at high strain rates, cryogenic temperatures, near-melting temperatures, or after heat treatments that alter the microstructure.
Observing substantial dislocation pile-up and strong work hardening in the single-phase control would falsify the proposed dominance of facile glide and dynamic recovery.
